title: The Trapped Insight

scenario.situation: The sales team wants warehouse-defined customer segments surfaced inside the CRM for outbound campaigns. A junior analyst is hand-exporting CSVs every Monday morning and uploading them manually. Leadership is debating whether to keep that process or assign an engineer to build a custom sync service.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The VP of Sales believes this is a one-off ops problem — either the CSV export becomes someone's standing duty, or engineering builds a dedicated pipeline for Outboundly's exact CRM and warehouse combination.
scenario.question: What is the right way to get warehouse segments into the CRM reliably and scalably?

decisions.prompt: The VP wants a solution by end of sprint. How do you frame your investigation before recommending anything?

options.label: Scope the custom build
options.detail: Gather engineering requirements to spec out a bespoke sync service between the warehouse and CRM.
options.consequence: You've anchored on the VP's framing before asking whether the problem is already solved elsewhere. You'll produce a thorough spec for something that may be unnecessary.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the stakeholder's proposed solution before auditing the solution space.

options.label: Diagnostic audit of the integration pattern
options.detail: Before choosing a solution, characterize what the workflow actually requires — what data moves, how often, to which destination — and ask whether this pattern has been solved before.
options.consequence: You map the workflow: a warehouse model needs to sync on a schedule to a CRM object. That description matches a well-known integration class. You now have the right question to evaluate solutions against.

options.label: Optimize the CSV export process
options.detail: Automate the Monday export with a cron job and email delivery to reduce manual effort.
options.consequence: You've made a brittle process slightly less painful. The data is still stale between runs, errors are still silent, and the CRM still depends on a file attachment nobody monitors.
options.divergenceCost: Polished a broken process instead of questioning whether the process should exist.

options.label: Survey the sales team on their segment needs
options.detail: Collect requirements from sales reps to understand which segments they want before deciding anything technical.
options.consequence: Useful for later prioritization, but requirements gathering doesn't resolve the delivery mechanism question. You still don't know how to get any segment — simple or complex — into the CRM reliably.
options.divergenceCost: Deferred the architectural question by collecting requirements for a delivery method still undefined.

decisions.prompt: You've characterized the workflow. Now you want to compare solutions. Which view of the data best reveals the right choice?

artifact.title: Estimated engineering effort to implement each approach (days)
artifact.caption: Raw effort estimates. Custom build looks dominant in cost — but effort alone doesn't show ongoing maintenance burden or failure risk.

options.label: Initial engineering effort (days to ship)
options.detail: Rank solutions by how long they take to implement the first time.
options.consequence: The custom build looks expensive up front, but the CSV export looks almost free. You'd be tempted to keep the export — without ever seeing that it silently fails, produces stale data, and creates a recurring manual burden that compounds over time.
options.divergenceCost: Compared only build cost, hiding the ongoing failure and maintenance cost that changes the ranking.

options.label: Total operational cost across dimensions (effort + reliability + maintenance)
options.detail: Score each solution on initial effort, ongoing maintenance burden, failure visibility, and data freshness — the factors that determine real operational cost.
options.consequence: When you normalize across dimensions, the CSV export and custom build collapse: high cumulative cost, silent failures, and no monitoring. The reverse ETL tool scores low on all cost dimensions — it is purpose-built for exactly this pattern and needs no custom code to maintain.

artifact.title: Operational cost score by solution (lower = better; composite of effort, maintenance, reliability)
artifact.caption: Composite score across initial effort, recurring maintenance, failure visibility, and data freshness. Reverse ETL dominates once all dimensions are counted.

decisions.prompt: The multi-dimensional view points clearly to reverse ETL. What do you tell the VP of Sales?

options.label: "Stop the CSV exports and cancel the custom build — reverse ETL solves this."
options.detail: Make the call and recommend immediate adoption.
options.consequence: You're probably right on the pattern, but you've skipped vendor evaluation, security review, and a pilot. If the chosen tool has a gap — unsupported CRM version, cost surprise, data governance constraint — you've already committed the org.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed readiness by skipping vendor fit validation before recommending adoption.

options.label: "The CSV export is the wrong long-term solution, and a custom build solves a problem that's already been solved — this fits a known pattern called reverse ETL. I'd recommend piloting a purpose-built tool against your CRM before committing."
options.detail: Name the pattern, show the evidence, and recommend a scoped pilot to confirm fit.
options.consequence: You've reframed the VP's two options as a false dilemma, introduced a known solution class with evidence, and proposed a low-risk path to validate it. The recommendation is confident and appropriately bounded.

insight: The team was debating two options — keep the manual export or build something custom — without asking whether the pattern was already solved. Reverse ETL is a well-established tool category purpose-built to push warehouse models into operational systems like CRMs. The real skill wasn't engineering; it was recognizing the integration pattern before speccing a solution, and evaluating options on total operational cost rather than just build effort. Naming a known pattern — and recommending a pilot rather than a leap — is what separates an analytics engineer from a ticket-taker.
